verses.verse:
षण्णाम् स्वराणाम् जनकः षड्जाख्यः खरो मतः।
तेनैव भावस्य पूर्तिः स्याच्छब्दानाम् क्रियया यथा।११५।
verses.text: The note called ṣaḍja is held to be the begetter of the six [other] notes. By it alone is the bhāva (feeling) completed, as [the sense of] words is by the verb.

commentary.text: When we accept some nāda (sound) as Sa, then the remaining notes have to be fixed on its basis. So the full name of Sa has been given as ṣaḍja, that is, the one that gives birth to the six. Just as in any language the sense of the other words depends on the verb, in the same way in music too the sense of all the notes is completed only on Sa. If one does not rest on Sa, the ālāpa will seem meaningless. Understood roughly, ālāpa or svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) rests on just three main actions: movement in some notes, rest on some notes, and the full stop on Sa. Just as in conversation many pauses are expected, from the comma to the full stop, in the same way in ālāpa too there are four kinds of pause: nyāsa, apanyāsa, vinyāsa and sanyāsa. Human life too is furnished with movement and pauses. Although man projects only the bhāva (feeling) in his heart onto notes and tāla, and, seeing life as ascent, descent and sthāī (steady state), sees his own bhāva reflected in the mirror of the notes, still it is a practical truth that going from Sa to komal Re gives the feeling of karuṇa rasa (pathos), and going to śuddha Re gives the feeling of śānta rasa (calm). And on returning to Sa again, that feeling becomes more vivid, as it were, and makes its impression on the listeners. So the effect of all the notes is held to arise from Sa alone: the nearer a note is to Sa, the more bhāva it can bring out, and the effect of a note far from Sa grows faint. So to keep that effect fresh, Pañcama and Madhyama make the contribution of Sa itself. This is the meaning of the following śloka.
